Question 1: Compare KNN and logistic regression

Use breast-cancer.csv, which contains 569 cases from the Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer dataset. Predict y (1 for malignant and 0 for benign) using mean_radius, mean_texture, and mean_smoothness.

Set a random seed and randomly split the observations into 70% training and 30% test data. Use the same split for every model. Standardize the predictors using the training means and standard deviations, and apply the same transformations to the test data.

Fit ordinary logistic regression with an intercept and no penalty, and KNN with Euclidean distance, equal neighbor weights, and

k∈{5,15,25,35,45}. k\in\{5,15,25,35,45\}.

Using the estimated probabilities for y = 1 on the test data, plot all six ROC curves in one figure and report their AUC values. Which of the six fitted models do you prefer? Give a brief justification based on your results.

Answer 1

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, roc_auc_score

seed = 43206
data = np.genfromtxt("data/breast-cancer.csv", delimiter=",", names=True)
X = np.column_stack([data[name] for name in
                     ["mean_radius", "mean_texture", "mean_smoothness"]])
y = data["y"].astype(int)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.30, random_state=seed
)
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test = scaler.transform(X_test)

models = {"Logistic regression": LogisticRegression(
    C=np.inf, fit_intercept=True, max_iter=1000
)}
models.update({f"KNN (k={k})": KNeighborsClassifier(
    n_neighbors=k, weights="uniform", metric="euclidean"
) for k in [5, 15, 25, 35, 45]})

print(f"Seed: {seed}; training: {len(y_train)}; test: {len(y_test)}")
Seed: 43206; training: 398; test: 171
print(f"{'Model':<22} {'Test AUC':>8}")
Model                  Test AUC
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
auc_values = {}
for name, model in models.items():
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    probabilities = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, probabilities)
    auc_values[name] = roc_auc_score(y_test, probabilities)
    print(f"{name:<22} {auc_values[name]:8.4f}")
    ax.plot(fpr, tpr, label=f"{name}: AUC = {auc_values[name]:.4f}")

Results and explanation:

I prefer logistic regression because it has the highest test AUC (0.9857), slightly above the best KNN model (k=45k=45, AUC 0.9834). In the same time it is a rather simpler model with only three predictors.

Question 2: Training and test ROC curves

Use the same data, training/test split, and standardization as in Question 1. Fit KNN with Euclidean distance, equal neighbor weights, and

k∈{1,3,5,10,20}. k\in\{1,3,5,10,20\}.

Use each fitted model to estimate probabilities for both the training and test observations. For training predictions, include each observation itself among its kk nearest neighbors.

For each kk, use a separate panel to show the training and test ROC curves together. Report both AUC values.

Explain the difference between training and test performance and how it changes with kk. In particular, explain what happens at k=1k=1 and why training performance may not reflect performance on new observations.

Answer 2

# Reuse the training/test split and standardized predictors from Question 1.
k_values = [1, 3, 5, 10, 20]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(12, 8), sharex=True, sharey=True)
print(f"{'k':>3} {'Training AUC':>14} {'Test AUC':>10}")
  k   Training AUC   Test AUC
q2_auc = {}

for k, ax in zip(k_values, axes.flat):
    model = KNeighborsClassifier(
        n_neighbors=k, weights="uniform", metric="euclidean"
    )
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    # Passing X_train explicitly includes each point itself as a neighbor.
    train_probs = model.predict_proba(X_train)[:, 1]
    test_probs = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    train_auc = roc_auc_score(y_train, train_probs)
    test_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, test_probs)
    q2_auc[k] = (train_auc, test_auc)
    print(f"{k:3d} {train_auc:14.4f} {test_auc:10.4f}")

    for label, labels, probs, auc in [
        ("Training", y_train, train_probs, train_auc),
        ("Test", y_test, test_probs, test_auc)
    ]:
        fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(labels, probs)
        ax.plot(fpr, tpr, label=f"{label}: AUC = {auc:.4f}")
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", alpha=0.4)
    ax.set(title=f"KNN (k={k})", xlabel="False positive rate",
           ylabel="True positive rate", xlim=(0, 1), ylim=(0, 1.02))
    ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8)

Results and explanation:

At k=1k=1, each training observation is its own nearest neighbor, so its estimated probability equals its label and training AUC is 1.0000. Test AUC is only 0.8896, showing overfitting. As kk increases to 20, averaging more neighbors smooths predictions: test AUC rises to 0.9806 and the training–test gap nearly disappears. Training AUC generally decreases, though not monotonically. Training performance is optimistic because it reuses observations used to fit the model; test performance better reflects predictions on new observations.
